title: Where to keep your savings
blurb: Drawer, savings account, fixed deposit or recurring deposit? Learn the trade-off between safety, access and interest.
t1.title: Safety, access and interest
t1.hook: Meena has {amt} saved. Her uncle says keep it in the steel cupboard. Her friend says use a bank. Who is right?
t1.define: Three things matter. **Safety**: will it be there? **Access**: can you get it fast? **Interest**: does it grow? No place wins at all three.
t1.analogy: Parking a scooter: outside your door is easy to reach but less safe. A guarded lot is safer, but you walk and wait.
q1.prompt: Meena's cash sits in a drawer at home. What can go wrong?
q1.hint: Think about theft, fire, and how easy it is to dip into.
q1.explain: Cash at home is the easiest to reach, but it has the weakest safety and earns no interest.
q1.opt.a: Nothing, only she knows about it
q1.fb.a: Hidden is not the same as safe. Cash at home can be lost, stolen or burnt, and it is easy to spend without thinking.
q1.opt.b: It can be lost, stolen or spent by habit, and it earns nothing
q1.opt.d: It loses all its value in a week
q2.prompt: What is the word for how quickly you can turn savings into cash?
q2.hint: It is about speed and ease, not about growth.
q2.explain: Access, or liquidity, is how fast and how cheaply you can reach your money.
t2.title: What the money earns
t2.define: **Interest** is what a bank pays you for keeping your money with it. The **rate** is the yearly share, shown as a percentage.
t2.formula: Simple interest = amount × rate × years. Compound amount = amount × (1 + rate) ^ years, so interest also earns interest.
t2.steps.1: Say Asha keeps {exAmt} where the rate is {exRate} a year.
t2.steps.2: After one year, the simple interest is {exInt}.
t2.steps.3: With compound interest, next year that {exInt} earns interest too.
q3.prompt: A savings account pays {saveRate} a year. How much simple interest does Meena's {amt} earn in one year?
q3.hint: Amount times rate times years. Here years is 1.
q4.prompt: Meena puts {amt} in a fixed deposit at {fdRate} a year, compounded yearly, for {fdYears} years. What is it worth at the end?
q4.hint: Amount times (1 + rate), then again for each year. Use the formula card above.
q4.explain: {amt} grows by {fdRate} each year for {fdYears} years. It becomes {fdAmount}.
t3.title: Deposits with a promise
t3.fd: In a **fixed deposit** you lock a sum for a set time at a set rate. Take it out early and you usually pay a **penalty**.
t3.rd: In a **recurring deposit** you put in a fixed amount every month for a set time. It suits people who earn a little each month.
t3.mistake: Many people think a fixed deposit can be withdrawn any time at no cost. Usually it cannot: breaking it early costs you part of the interest.
q5.prompt: Meena breaks her {amt} fixed deposit early. The penalty is {penalty} of the amount. How much does she lose?
q6.prompt: Which statement about a fixed deposit is true?
q6.hint: Remember the word "fixed". What is fixed about it?
q6.explain: A fixed deposit trades access for a set rate. Early exit usually costs you.
q6.opt.a: You can take the money out any time with no cost
q6.fb.a: Locked means locked. Taking it out early usually means a penalty, so the money is not fully free to use.
q6.opt.b: It gives a set rate, but leaving early usually costs you
q6.opt.d: You must keep adding money every month
q7.prompt: Ravi puts {rdMonthly} into a recurring deposit every month for {rdMonths} months at {rdRate} a year. How much interest does he earn in all?
q7.hint: He ends with about {rdFinal}. Take away what he put in: {rdTotal}.
q7.explain: He puts in {rdTotal} and ends with {rdFinal}. The interest is {rdEarned}.
t4.title: Lab: simple or compound
t4.explore: Open the lab. Change the rate and the years to see how simple and compound growth drift apart. Then answer below.
q8.prompt: In the lab, set the rate to {labRate} and the years to {labYears}. What does the {amt} become with compound interest?
q8.hint: Read the green number in the lab.
q9.prompt: With the same settings, how much extra does compounding give compared with simple interest?
q9.hint: Read the Extra from compounding box in the lab.
q9.explain: Compounding gives {labExtra} more, because interest also earns interest.
t5.title: Match the place to the need
t5.tradeoff: Cash at home is easy to reach but weak on safety and interest. Locked deposits pay more but cost you access. Pick by when you need the money.
t5.note: Rates here are made up to practise. Real rates change, so always check before you decide. Savings and investing also differ in risk and goal.
q10.prompt: Ravi needs exam fees in three weeks. Where should that money sit?
q10.hint: He needs it soon. Which place lets him reach it fast, without a penalty?
q10.explain: Money needed soon belongs where it is safe and easy to reach. A savings account fits.
q10.opt.a: A fixed deposit that ends in five years
q10.opt.b: A savings account, safe and easy to reach
q10.opt.c: With a neighbour who promises to give it back
q10.opt.d: A recurring deposit that ends in three years
glossary.save_interest.def: Money a bank pays you for keeping your money with it.
glossary.save_fixed_deposit.def: A sum locked for a set time at a set rate.
glossary.save_recurring_deposit.def: A fixed amount put in every month for a set time.
glossary.save_access.def: How quickly and cheaply you can turn savings into cash.
glossary.save_penalty.def: A charge for taking a locked deposit out before its end date.
